items.title: Mahama commissions Christian Tetteh Yohuno Ward Complex at Police Hospital
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has commissioned an 85-bed ward complex at the Police Hospital in Accra, named after the Inspector General of Police (IGP), Christian Tetteh Yohuno. The facility, commissioned on Tuesday, October 13, under the theme: “ Christian Tetteh Yohuno Ward Complex ”, was constructed to commemorate the Golden Jubilee celebration of the Police Hospital and is fully equipped with ultramodern healthcare facilities. President Mahama described the new facility as an important investment in the health and welfare of personnel of the Ghana Police Service and a significant enhancement to the hospital’s capacity to serve the wider Ghanaian public. He recalled that nearly a year ago, he joined the IGP and the Police Management Board at the Police Training School in Tesano for the Police Remembrance Day observance, during which officers who died in the line of duty were honoured and solidarity was shown to their families. The President said that on that solemn occasion he discussed with the IGP the need to pay greater attention to the welfare of serving police officers. “And today, we see a tangible outcome of that discussion. I commend the Inspector General of Police and the Police Management Board for their leadership in delivering this new hospital block, which is equipped with the most modern facilities,” he stated. President Mahama also expressed appreciation to the health professionals and all those whose efforts contributed to the successful completion of the project. He noted that men and women of the Ghana Police Service undertake difficult and often dangerous assignments, including responding to emergencies, confronting violent crime and maintaining peace and security in communities. According to him, the demands of policing affect both the physical and mental well-being of officers, making it imperative for them to have access to timely and high-quality healthcare whenever they are injured or fall ill. The President said the responsibility of the State also extended to supporting the families of officers, whose sacrifices often enable them to perform their duties effectively. “An officer’s ability to protect the public is closely linked to the support the police service provides. Access to appropriate healthcare is therefore essential for operational readiness,” the President said. President Mahama disclosed that even before the formal commissioning of the facility, seven police officers who sustained injuries in the line of duty in Bunkpurugu and Porto had been admitted to the new ward complex. He said the officers had been transported to Accra and were receiving treatment at the facility. He said they would get the best care at the new facility. The President stated that the new block would strengthen the hospital’s capacity to provide quality healthcare services, particularly for officers injured in the line of duty and patients requiring urgent medical attention. He also underscored the importance of addressing the psychological impact of policing, noting that repeated exposure to violence, tragedy and distress could have lasting effects on officers. He said mental health support, counselling and appropriate treatment should be readily accessible without fear of stigma. “When officers know that their health and welfare is being taken seriously, they can serve with greater confidence and focus. Investing in their care strengthens our collective national security.” President Mahama noted that the Police Hospital’s role extended beyond serving police personnel, as it formed part of Ghana’s national healthcare system and provided emergency medical services to the public. He said the expanded facility would help strengthen healthcare delivery, particularly during emergencies, road accidents and public health crises. The President emphasised that every patient who visited the hospital deserved to be treated with dignity and compassion. He stated that the true value of the facility would be measured by the quality of healthcare provided and how well it was maintained over time. President Mahama therefore urged the hospital’s management to uphold the highest standards of hygiene, patient safety and clinical practice. He stressed the need for regular maintenance of medical equipment, uninterrupted availability of essential medicines and supplies, and continuous capacity-building for healthcare personnel. The President also commended the doctors, nurses, pharmacists, laboratory technicians and support staff who would serve in the new block. “And behind every patient record is a person who may be frightened, in pain, or uncertain about their future,” he said. “And so, when you are confronted with such patients, listen to them carefully, explain to them clearly, and treat every patient with the respect you would wish for your own family.” President Mahama reiterated the Government’s commitment to improving the safety, welfare and operational effectiveness of personnel of the Ghana Police Service. The Minister for the Interior, Muntaka Mohammed-Mubarak, said President Mahama’s commitment to improving healthcare infrastructure and enhancing the welfare of security personnel continued to leave a lasting impact on the nation. He said the facility stood as a visible symbol of the President’s dedication to building a stronger and more inclusive Ghana. The IGP, on his part, expressed gratitude to President Mahama for his continuous support for the Police Service and his concern for the welfare of officers. He assured that the Police Administration would continue to pursue initiatives aimed at improving the health, welfare and operational effectiveness of personnel of the Service.

items.title: Vice President calls for wider access to Ghana’s political party histories
items.description: Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has called for wider access to publications documenting Ghana’s political party histories, stressing the importance of historical knowledge in deepening public understanding of the country’s governance institutions and constitutional arrangements. She said making such records accessible to the public would enable citizens to better understand the political experiences that have shaped the Republic and equip them to participate more meaningfully in the country’s political life. Speaking at the launch of six historiographies of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) on Tuesday, October 13, the Vice President emphasised that knowledge of political history should not be confined to people who experienced the events first-hand. According to her, documenting the country’s political journey and making the resulting publications widely available would help preserve important historical records for present and future generations. “Familiarity with our governance institutions, with our constitutional arrangements, and the political experiences that have shaped our Republic” is important for meaningful civic participation, she said. Professor Opoku-Agyemang explained that citizens who have access to such knowledge are better positioned to understand the institutions and processes that govern the country, as well as the historical developments that have influenced Ghana’s political system. She noted that historical understanding should extend beyond those who lived through particular political periods, arguing that younger generations and other members of the public should also have opportunities to learn from the country’s political experiences. “When that knowledge is accessible, citizens are better placed to participate meaningfully in political life. The knowledge of history is also not restricted to those who have lived through it,” she added. The Vice President expressed the hope that the newly launched publications would be distributed to a broad range of institutions and individuals to ensure that the historical accounts reach a wider audience. “It is my hope that these publications will reach libraries, research institutions, private spaces, and public officials too,” she said. She also encouraged regional and constituency executives of the NDC to keep copies of the publications in their offices, alongside other important historical documents. According to her, making the books available at the party’s various organisational levels would provide members and visitors with opportunities to engage with the party’s history and learn more about the developments that have shaped its evolution. The launch of the six historiographies provides an opportunity to preserve accounts of the NDC’s political journey and make them available for research, institutional reference and public education. The publications, she indicated, should therefore be treated as important reference materials that can contribute to a deeper understanding of Ghana’s governance structures, constitutional development and political experiences.

items.title: Lutte contre la corruption : La HAPLUCIA lance une leçon inaugurale à l’ENA pour promouvoir l’intégrité
items.description: Lomé, 13 oct. (ATOP) – La Haute autorité de prévention et de lutte contre la corruption et les infractions assimilées (HAPLUCIA) a lancé, le mardi 13 octobre à l’École nationale d’administration (ENA) à Lomé, une leçon inaugurale consacrée à l’éthique, à l’intégrité et à la lutte contre la corruption. Cette initiative marque l’extension du projet d’intégration de l’éducation à la lutte contre la corruption dans les programmes d’enseignement et de formation au Togo, après une phase de prétest dans plusieurs établissements d’enseignement supérieur. La leçon est placée sous le thème « Servir l’État et les citoyens avec intégrité : éducation à la citoyenneté, éthique administrative et lutte contre la corruption ». Elle vise à renforcer les valeurs républicaines et le sens de l’intérêt général chez les futurs cadres de l’État. Le président de la HAPLUCIA, Aba Kimélabalou a souligné que la prévention durable de la corruption repose sur l’éducation et la formation des consciences, tout au long du parcours académique et professionnel. S’appuyant sur les enquêtes de l’institution, il a cité parmi les causes perçues du phénomène, le niveau modeste des salaires et des revenus (42,6 %), la cupidité (23,7 %), l’impunité (21,1 %) et la pauvreté (17 %). La transparence, le contrôle interne, la numérisation et la dématérialisation des services publics ont été présentés comme des moyens de réduire les possibilités de fraude. M. Aba Kimelabalou a également rappelé les conséquences de la corruption à savoir : la perte des ressources publiques, la dégradation des services, le recul de la confiance citoyenne et l’injustice sociale. Il a exhorté les élèves des cycles 2 et 3 à faire preuve de probité, de rigueur et de redevabilité et à résister aux sollicitations illicites et aux pressions de toute nature. « Le Togo a besoin d’une administration compétente, mais surtout d’une administration digne de confiance », a-t-il déclaré. Le directeur de l’ENA, Prof. Adama Kpodar a estimé que la lutte contre la corruption devait aussi agir sur les mentalités et les valeurs des futurs agents publics. Le programme selon lui, vise à doter les élèves administrateurs des outils intellectuels et moraux nécessaires pour résister aux tentations tout au long de leur parcours professionnel, en formant les consciences, en agissant sur le système et en pérennisant l’engagement. Par ce projet, la HAPLUCIA et l’ENA entendent faire de l’institution administrative, un pôle d’excellence moral et professionnel, afin de contribuer à une administration publique plus transparente, efficace et tournée vers le service des citoyens. ATOP/SED/JK

items.title: Tinubu writes Senate, forwards 5 bills on drug enforcement, transport, others
items.description: By Henry Umoru President Bola Tinubu has written the Senate, transmitting a series of bills for consideration and the bills include proposed legislation to amend the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Act, establish a National School of Government and reform the legal framework governing the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, among others. The bills, in accordance with the provisions of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, were conveyed by the President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio. The Executive communications were read on Tuesday by Akpabio. One of the proposals, the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Amendment Bill 2026, seeks to amend the existing 2022 Act to reposition the bureau as an independent authority and expand its mandate. The proposed amendment also seeks to transfer supervisory oversight of the bureau to the Presidency, alongside changes to its administrative structure. According to the letter, “The Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Amendment Bill seeks to reposition the Bureau as an independent multimodal safety investigation authority, expanding its mandate beyond aviation to maritime and other transport occurrences. “It also proposes transferring the Bureau’s oversight to the Presidency and strengthening its institutional, operational, administrative and constitutional framework. Another proposal, the NDLEA Bill 2026, seeks to establish a consolidated legal framework for the operations of the NDLEA. The bill is expected to strengthen the agency’s powers, including its capacity to investigate individuals suspected of involvement in illicit drug-related activities. According to the letter, “The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Bill seeks to repeal the existing NDLEA Act and the Indian Hemp Act, both contained in the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. “The proposed legislation is intended to establish a consolidated legal framework for combating the cultivation, processing, trafficking and use of illicit drugs. “It also seeks to empower the agency to investigate persons suspected of involvement in drug-related activities.” President Tinubu also transmitted the National School of Government Bill (ASCON) 2026, which seeks to repeal the Administrative staff college of Nigeria act and establish a National School of Government. The proposed institution is intended to serve as a national centre for governance training, public sector capacity development and institutional strengthening. The National School of Government Bill seeks to repeal the Administrative Staff College of Nigeria Act and establish a new institution to serve as a national centre for leadership development, policy delivery and executive capacity-building. The President equally transmitted a bill seeking to domesticate the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their two Additional Protocols of 1977, which provide for the protection of victims of armed conflict, as well as the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, providing for the enforcement of punishment on genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. The letter reads further, “The Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols Bill seeks to repeal the existing Geneva Conventions Act and give effect in Nigeria to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the two Additional Protocols adopted in 1977. “The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Enforcement) Bill seeks to domesticate the Rome Statute and establish a framework for the enforcement and punishment of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and related offences. “It also provides for Nigeria’s cooperation with the International Criminal Court in the performance of its functions”. Akpabio thereafter referred the bills to the Committee on Rules and Business for further legislative action. Meanwhile, the Senate received notification of President Tinubu’s assent to two amendment bills providing for the inclusion of federal universities in Yaba, Lagos, and Kaduna in the relevant laws governing federal universities of technology. Akpabio said the Federal University of Technology Amendment No. 2 Bill, 2026, provides for the inclusion of the Federal University of Technology and Vocational Studies in Yaba in the relevant Act. “The Federal University of Technology Amendment Bill, 2026, seeks to amend the Federal Universities of Technology Act to include the Federal University of Technology and Vocational Studies in Kaduna”. He thereafter referred the documents to the Clerk to the National Assembly for further action. Akpabio commended Tinubu for assenting to the two bills, describing the development as an important step towards promoting education in Nigeria. items.title: NNPC’s 2026 revenue hits N28.5trn, jumps 21% in August
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Nigerian National Petroleum Company, NNPC, Limited recorded cumulative revenue of N28.54 trillion in the first eight months of 2026, with revenue rising by 21.1 per cent month-on-month to N3.74 trillion in August. Read Also: NAF Plane Crash: Igbokoda residents lament stench, fear disease outbreak, as body parts float The company’s August 2026 Monthly Report Summary showed that revenue increased from N3.087 trillion in July to N3.737 trillion in August, while profit after tax rose by 54.5 per cent to N431 billion from N279 billion in the preceding month. An analysis of the company’s reports in 2026 indicated that NNPC generated N2.571 trillion in January, N2.680 trillion in February and N2.774 trillion in March before revenue surged to N4.971 trillion in April. Revenue subsequently stood at N4.335 trillion in May and N4.389 trillion in June before declining to N3.087 trillion in July and recovering in August. The monthly figures showed that profit after tax stood at N385 billion in January, N236 billion in February, N276 billion in March, N481 billion in April, N462 billion in May and N535 billion in June before falling to N279 billion in July and rebounding to N431 billion in August. Cumulatively, the company’s profit after tax amounted to N2.985 trillion in the first eight months of the year. NNPC’s statutory payments to the government in August was N1.574 trillion bringing total payment to N9.487 trillion in 2026. On production, the report put average crude oil and condensate output at 1.69 million barrels per day in August, slightly higher than the 1.68 million barrels per day recorded in July. Natural gas production stood at 7,680 million standard cubic feet per day in August, up from 7,489 million standard cubic feet per day in July. However, the August figure was below the 7,841 million standard cubic feet per day recorded in June, the highest level shown in the 12-month production chart. Gas sales increased to 4,737 million standard cubic feet per day in August from 4,581 million standard cubic feet per day in July. Similarly, crude oil and condensate sales rose to 24.56 million barrels in August from 22.53 million barrels in July. NNPC reported 100 per cent availability of upstream pipelines, adding that Obiafu-Obrikom-Oben (OB3) gas pipeline project had reached 100 per cent completion, while the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) gas pipeline was 95 per cent complete. On the AKK project, NNPC said construction and installation activities were continuing, with the objective of delivering gas to Abuja in 2026. For the OB3 pipeline, the company reported a major milestone with the successful commissioning and full operationalisation of the pipeline, which is intended to link the eastern and western gas network systems. items.title: Présidence de la République : Tebboune nomme Lounès Magramane directeur de cabinet
items.description: Le successeur de feu Boualem Boualem au poste de directeur de cabinet de la présidence de la République est connu. Il s’agit de Lounès Magramane, qui occupait jusque-là les fonctions de secrétaire général du ministère des Affaires étrangères. L'annonce de la nomination de M. Magramane a été faite ce mardi 13 octobre par la présidence de la République. “Le président de la République, M. Abdelmadjid Tebboune , a nommé aujourd’hui M. Lounès Magramane au poste de directeur du cabinet de la présidence de la République”, a indiqué la présidence sur sa page Facebook officielle. Lounès Magramane, qui est le nouveau chef de cabinet de la Présidence de la République ? Lounès Magramane succède à Boualem Boualem, décédé le 5 octobre à Genève. Boualem Boualem était en poste depuis novembre 2023. Lounès Magramane avait été nommé secrétaire général du ministère des Affaires étrangères en juin 2023. Il avait succédé à Amar Belani. Né en 1961 à Boumerdès, Lounès Magramane est un diplomate de carrière, diplômé de l’Ecole nationale d’administration (ENA), section diplomatie. Il a notamment occupé plusieurs postes dans l'administration centrale du ministère des Affaires étrangères et était ambassadeur d’Algérie à Londres (2021-2023), aux Pays-Bas (2019-2021), en Hongrie (2009-2015) et au Niger (2001-2005). items.title: Infantino received undisclosed $1.72m World Cup payment — Reports
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Embattled FIFA president Gianni Infantino received a previously undisclosed $1.72 million payment from the organisation responsible for managing the 2026 World Cup, according to FIFA and US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) documents obtained by ESPN. According to the report published on Tuesday, the lack of transparency surrounding the compensation raises questions over compliance with FIFA statutes, which require the individual compensation of the organisation’s president to be made public. The payment was made in 2024 by FWC2026, the US-based entity established by FIFA to manage and operate the 2026 World Cup, according to IRS records. The $1.72 million compensation was in addition to Infantino’s regular salary and benefits from FIFA, which amounted to 4.274 million Swiss francs, or approximately $4.86 million, in 2024, according to the organisation’s financial report. The additional payment was not disclosed in FIFA’s 2024 annual report, the latest year for which FWC2026’s IRS Form 990 is publicly available, ESPN reported. Article 43, paragraph 13 of FIFA’s statutes states that the organisation’s Compensation Sub-Committee determines the compensation of the FIFA president, council members and secretary general, adding that their individual compensation “shall be made public”. However, FIFA has denied violating its disclosure obligations, insisting that its financial reporting complies with applicable requirements. A FIFA spokesperson told ESPN that the organisation “fully complies with all reporting requirements and strongly rejects any suggestion there has been a violation of FIFA’s Statutes”. In a separate statement, the spokesperson said FIFA did not pay Infantino a second salary and that his annual compensation and other contractual benefits were determined by the independent Compensation Sub-Committee. “FIFA strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated FIFA’s Statutes,” the spokesperson said, adding that FIFA’s accounts were independently audited and its declarations complied with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere. The Times first reported Infantino’s additional compensation from FWC2026 and the questions surrounding its disclosure. Miguel Maduro, former chairman of FIFA’s governance committee, told the newspaper that failing to make additional payments from FIFA-related entities public would contravene the organisation’s transparency rules. Maduro argued that FIFA’s statutes imposed an obligation of full transparency, adding that the compensation committee should not authorise alternative forms of remuneration that were not publicly disclosed. The latest revelation adds to the scrutiny surrounding Infantino, who has faced criticism over his leadership and a proposal earlier this year to sell a 20 per cent stake in the World Cup to private investors. The proposed investment plan, which Infantino reportedly called FIFA Forward Enterprise, drew opposition from football officials concerned about transparency and the management of the sport’s commercial interests. Infantino has also faced pressure following his close relationship with US President Donald Trump ahead of the 2026 World Cup, which was hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico. The FIFA president is expected to meet members of the FIFA Council in Zurich on Thursday, amid continuing discussions about the organisation’s governance and financial arrangements. Infantino has confirmed plans to seek re-election in March 2027, despite criticism from some football officials over his leadership. items.title: Sénat : Deux lois soumises en deuxième lecture
items.description: Lomé, 13 oct. (ATOP) – Deux lois soumises en deuxième lecture au Sénat ont été adoptées, le mardi 13 octobre à Lomé lors de la 2 ème séance plénière de la 2 ème session ordinaire de l’année 2026. Les travaux ont été dirigés par le président du Sénat, Barry Moussa Barqué, en présence du ministre délégué auprès du ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération et des Togolais de l’extérieur, chargé de la Coopération et des Togolais de l’extérieur, Yackoley Kokou Johnson. Il s’agit en effet de la loi autorisant la ratification de la convention portant création de l’organisation internationale pour la médiation, adoptée le 30 mai 2025 à Hong Kong et la loi portant budget du Sénat, exercice 2027. L’adoption des lois La première loi autorisant la ratification de la convention vise à promouvoir le recours à la médiation pour le règlement pacifique de différends internationaux. Pour le Togo, la ratification ouvrirait la possibilité de participer aux travaux de l’organisation et d’accéder, dans le respect des règles conventionnelles, à ses mécanismes de médiation et de renforcement des capacités. Pour le président Barqué, le rôle actif du Togo dans les initiatives de médiation, illustre sa capacité à contribuer à la stabilité régionale. « Cette responsabilité renforce l’image du Togo comme partenaire fiable et promoteur de la coopération internationale. La ratification de cette convention exige une participation active aux travaux de l’organisation, une appropriation des principes qu’elle porte et un engagement constant en faveur de la paix », a indiqué le président du Sénat. Selon le ministre Yackoley Johnson, l’adoption de cette loi renforce l’engagement du Togo en faveur de la prévention des conflits, du règlement pacifique des différends et de la promotion du dialogue entre les États. « Le choix d’adhérer à l’Organisation internationale pour la médiation témoigne la volonté de notre pays à contribuer activement et plus que jamais au renforcement de la confiance mutuelle, à la consolidation de la paix et au développement de la coopération internationale à travers des approches consensuelles de règlement des différends », a affirmé le ministre. L’adoption de la loi portant budget du Sénat exercice 2027 a été débattue à huis clos. ATOP/AR/SED

items.title: 4-year courses must end in 4 years, Alausa tells varsities
items.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The federal government has pledged to honour its agreements with tertiary institution workers, declaring that Nigerian students must no longer lose precious academic years to strikes triggered by unfulfilled government commitments. Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, gave the assurance on Tuesday in Abuja while unveiling the 2026 agreements between the Federal Government and staff unions in universities, polytechnics and colleges of education. Alausa, who described the agreements as a major step towards restoring confidence in government-union relations, said the administration of President Bola Tinubu was determined to end the cycle of broken promises, industrial disputes and disruptions to academic calendars that had plagued the country’s tertiary education system for decades. He declared that a four-year degree programme must be completed in four years, insisting that the Federal Government would fulfil its obligations under the newly unveiled agreements. “During his campaign, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu promised that a four-year course would be completed in four years. Today, through his leadership, these agreements give practical expression to that pledge: A promise made, a promise kept, and trust restored,” the minister said. The agreements cover the Consolidated Academic Tools Allowance, CATA, for the Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics, ASUP, and the Colleges of Education Academic Staff Union, COEASU, as well as the Consolidated Non-Teaching Tools Allowance, CONTTA, for non-teaching staff unions across universities, polytechnics and colleges of education. The allowances are to take effect from January 1, 2026, in line with the agreements and applicable implementation guidelines. Alausa, however, acknowledged that the unveiling of the agreements was only the beginning, stressing that their credibility would ultimately depend on the government’s ability to implement the provisions faithfully. “Let me state clearly, on behalf of the Federal Government: We will fulfil our own part of these historic agreements. We recognise that public confidence will depend on the obligations we honour after this ceremony,” he said. In a move aimed at preventing future disputes over the implementation of agreements, the minister announced the expansion of the existing Implementation and Monitoring Committee, IMC, established for the agreement with the Academic Staff Union of Universities, ASUU. Under the new arrangement, the committee will become a single monitoring platform for agreements with academic and non-academic staff unions across tertiary institutions. Its membership will be broadened to accommodate the relevant unions and stakeholders, with responsibility for tracking agreed milestones, assessing progress, resolving implementation challenges and ensuring accountability through periodic reports. According to Alausa, the committee will monitor both achievements and outstanding obligations to ensure that commitments are implemented within agreed timelines. He said the government intended to identify implementation difficulties early and resolve them before they degenerated into disputes capable of disrupting academic activities. The minister urged government agencies to discharge their responsibilities diligently, while governing councils and institutional managements were directed to maintain accurate records, comply with implementation guidelines and cooperate fully with the committee. He also urged union leaders to keep their members informed and channel emerging concerns through established mechanisms. Alausa recalled that agreements between successive governments and staff unions had, for decades, been undermined by delayed, incomplete or unfulfilled commitments, leading to recurring industrial disputes. The consequences, he said, extended beyond the negotiating parties, with students losing valuable learning time, families bearing additional financial burdens and teaching and research suffering repeated setbacks. He noted that prolonged strikes had created uncertainty around academic calendars, making it difficult for students to complete their programmes within the prescribed periods. The minister said the Tinubu administration was determined to reverse the trend by building a system in which agreements were respected and academic activities proceeded without unnecessary interruptions. He maintained that industrial harmony was indispensable to educational excellence, adding that stable academic calendars would enable institutions to plan effectively, sustain research and allow students to concentrate on their studies. “We must strengthen early consultation and resolve differences through constructive dialogue, mutual respect and good-faith engagement. Our students and their families must remain at the centre of these efforts,” he said. Explaining the significance of the agreements, Alausa said CATA and CONTTA were designed to support the professional and operational needs of eligible academic and non-academic personnel. He said the allowances reflected the government’s recognition that the quality of tertiary education was inseparable from the welfare, motivation and professional wellbeing of the workforce. According to him, improved staff welfare must go beyond financial allowances to include fair treatment, transparent promotion processes, occupational safety and opportunities for career advancement. He pledged that the Federal Ministry of Education would continue to work with relevant agencies, governing councils, institutional managements and unions to create an environment in which personnel could perform their duties effectively. The minister also commended the leadership of ASUP, COEASU and the non-teaching staff unions for their participation in the negotiations, while acknowledging the contributions of relevant ministries, departments, agencies and technical teams. Alausa reserved special commendation for the Federal Government Tertiary Institutions Expanded Negotiation Committee, chaired by Malam Yayale Ahmed, whose work he said had brought the negotiations to a successful conclusion. He praised Ahmed and members of the committee for their patience, experience and dedication in resolving the issues involved in the negotiations. The minister also credited President Tinubu’s support and guidance for making the agreements possible, describing them as evidence of the administration’s commitment to the welfare of education workers and the future of Nigerian students. Signed agreements were presented to representatives of academic and non-academic staff unions, including ASUP, COEASU, the Senior Staff Association of Nigerian Universities, SSANU, the Non-Academic Staff Union of Educational and Associated Institutions, NASU, the National Association of Academic Technologists, NAAT, and other unions representing staff in polytechnics and colleges of education. The ultimate test of the agreements, however, will be whether the allowances are implemented as stipulated and the monitoring mechanism can prevent outstanding obligations from triggering another round of industrial disputes. To prevent future disputes from escalating into industrial action, the Minister announced plans to expand the existing implementation and monitoring committee established for ASUU into a single body responsible for monitoring all agreements with academic and non-academic staff unions in tertiary institutions. He said the committee’s membership had been broadened to accommodate the unions and other relevant stakeholders, adding that the government would also work towards making it a permanent structure. According to him, the decision followed the success of having a single committee negotiate with the various unions, which helped accelerate the renegotiation process. He said the expanded panel would provide a platform for identifying implementation challenges early and resolving grievances before they disrupt academic activities. He urged union leaders to channel complaints through the committee rather than resorting to public confrontations or threats of strikes. Alausa added that the agreements contained a provision for review every three years, allowing the government and unions to reopen discussions on emerging concerns and mutually agreed adjustments. In his remarks, Ahmed who served as Permanent Secretary in the Federal Ministry of Education between 1997 and 2000, said the success of the negotiations depended on a spirit of give-and-take between the government and labour unions. According to him, union leaders demonstrated responsibility by defending their members’ interests while also appreciating the financial and administrative constraints facing the government. The elder statesman, however, stressed that unveiling the agreement was only the beginning, insisting that its successful implementation would be the real test of the negotiations. “To me, this is the beginning of our job. The most important thing is for us to have a seamless agreement collectively, which the government is not only willing but comfortable to implement to the letter,” he said. He expressed confidence in the commitment of Dr Alausa and the Minister of State for Education, Prof. Suwaiba Ahmad, to ensure that the pact was implemented, while commending President Tinubu for what he described as the political will to address longstanding challenges in the education sector. The negotiation chairman also disclosed that discrepancies had been identified in parts of the agreement, assuring the unions that the issues would be addressed in collaboration with the Ministry of Education and the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission. Earlier in their separate remarks, the National President, Academic Staff Union of Polytechnics, ASUP, Comrade Shammah Kpanja; his counterpart at the Colleges of Education Academic Staff Union, COEASU, Dr. Lawal Bazza; and the President of the Senior Staff Association of Nigerian Universities, SSANU, Comrade Ibrahim Mohammed, commended the Federal Government for the speedy renegotiation of the agreement and the progress made in its implementation. Kpanja described the process as the fastest in the history of the union’s negotiations, noting that talks began in December 2025 and culminated in the signing of the agreement in April 2026. He disclosed that implementation had commenced, with members receiving outstanding arrears between July and September, but urged the government to ensure that all other provisions of the agreement were fully implemented. He also welcomed the planned inauguration of a joint implementation committee, expressing hope that it would accelerate implementation before the end of the year. Similarly, Bazza said the Colleges of Education subsector had already achieved more than 70 per cent implementation of the agreement, expressing confidence that the committee would help address the outstanding provisions. items.title: Adam Mouak, le jeune gardien marocain convoqué par Luis Enrique
items.description: À seulement 17 ans, Adam Mouak figure dans le groupe de 23 joueurs du Paris Saint-Germain retenus par Luis Enrique pour affronter Manchester City, mardi soir, à l’Etihad Stadium, lors de la deuxième journée de la phase de ligue de la Ligue des champions. Une nouvelle étape pour le jeune portier marocain, formé au sein du club parisien. Le football marocain continue de se distinguer au Paris Saint-Germain. Le jeune gardien Adam Mouak a été convoqué par Luis Enrique pour le déplacement du club parisien sur la pelouse de Manchester City, prévu mardi 13 octobre, dans le cadre de la deuxième journée de la phase de ligue de la Ligue des champions. Âgé de 17 ans, le portier intègre le groupe professionnel parisien pour cette affiche européenne de premier plan. Formé au PSG depuis son enfance, il occupe actuellement le rôle de troisième gardien dans la hiérarchie de l’équipe première, derrière le Russe Matvey Safonov et le Français Lucas Chevalier. Le groupe pour le retour de la Ligue des champions ! Manchester #MICPSG I #UCL pic.twitter.com/RCE9dQQYYe — Paris Saint-Germain (@PSG_inside) October 13, 2026 Cette convocation intervient dans un contexte particulier, marqué par l’indisponibilité du gardien italien Alessandro Longoni, blessé depuis plusieurs semaines. L’absence de ce dernier a ainsi permis au jeune Marocain de rejoindre le groupe professionnel pour cette rencontre face aux Citizens, aux côtés notamment de son compatriote Achraf Hakimi. Cette première opportunité de figurer dans le groupe parisien pour une rencontre européenne majeure constitue une étape importante dans le parcours d’Adam Mouak. Le jeune gardien poursuit sa progression au centre de formation du PSG, tout en portant les couleurs du Maroc dans les catégories de jeunes. Il a notamment été convoqué avec la sélection marocaine U17 pour des stages de préparation et des matchs amicaux, avant de rejoindre les U18 à l’occasion d’un tournoi international organisé en Espagne en septembre dernier. Si cette convocation ne garantit pas une apparition sur le terrain, elle représente une occasion pour le portier de se rapprocher davantage du groupe professionnel et de découvrir les exigences du très haut niveau européen. items.title: Republic Bank JoyNews Habitat Fair to connect prospective homeowners with exhibitors in Ho from October 16 to 18
items.description: Financial constraints and difficulties saving enough money remain major obstacles for some prospective homeowners, as the Republic Bank JoyNews Habitat Fair prepares to open in Ho from October 16 to 18, 2026. The three-day event, scheduled for the Ho Sports Stadium, will connect prospective homeowners with exhibitors and give participants the opportunity to explore options related to construction, interior decoration, furniture, home security, and other aspects of home improvement. For Cecilia Asare, who currently lives with her parents, the cost of living independently remains a major concern. She said moving out without sufficient financial resources could leave her struggling to meet her basic needs. “Hmm, first, money. Second, if I leave my parents’ house, I’ll go hungry,” she said. Despite the financial challenges, Cecilia hopes to gain ideas from the fair on how to create a comfortable home that reflects her needs and personality. She said she would prefer interior designs and furniture that express who she is. “When it comes to the design, I’ll go for something that really talks about my personality. The moment it comes to my home, it should show you that this is who I am without talking so much,” she said. Another prospective homeowner, Michael Akomeah, identified saving towards a home as a challenge because of his existing investment commitments. “I’m doing some investment. That’s why,” he said, explaining why he had found it difficult to save towards homeownership. He welcomed the opportunity to participate in the fair, which is intended to help prospective homeowners explore products and services that could support their plans. The Republic Bank JoyNews Habitat Fair aims to bring prospective homeowners closer to their homeownership goals by connecting them with businesses and service providers across the housing industry. The event will run from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the Ho Sports Stadium, with activities scheduled from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. daily. Participants will have the opportunity to explore options in construction, interior decoration, furniture, home security and other home-related services. The fair is expected to provide a platform for prospective homeowners to discover available products and services as they work towards turning their homeownership aspirations into reality.

items.title: Interpellation d’un faux policier qui plaçait ses victimes en «garde à vue» chez lui
items.description: La Police républicaine du Bénin a annoncé, le mardi 13 octobre 2026, l’interpellation à Kétou d’un individu soupçonné d’avoir usurpé la qualité de policier pour soutirer 100 000 F CFA à une victime et d’avoir emmené une caissière avec la recette du jour d’une cafétéria. Une tenue camouflée a été découverte à son domicile. L’uniforme ne fait pas le policier. À Kétou, dans le sud-est du Bénin, un individu aurait décidé de s’affranchir de cette évidence en se faisant passer pour un agent des forces de l’ordre. Mais ses prétendues activités policières ont fini par attirer l’attention des véritables policiers, qui ont mis un terme à son entreprise présumée d’escroquerie. Selon les informations rendues publiques, ce mardi 13 octobre, par la Police républicaine, deux personnes se sont présentées au commissariat de l’arrondissement de Kétou, dimanche 11 octobre, pour dénoncer des faits d’escroquerie impliquant un individu qui se faisait passer pour un fonctionnaire de police. La première victime aurait été approchée par le suspect, qui lui aurait annoncé l’organisation prochaine d’une vente aux enchères dans l’enceinte du commissariat de Kétou. Convaincue par cette présentation, elle lui aurait remis la somme de 100 000 FCFA pour l’acquisition d’une moto. Mais ni la moto ni la vente annoncée n’ont été au rendez-vous. La seconde affaire concerne un tenancier de cafétéria de la localité. D’après les éléments communiqués par la Police républicaine, le suspect se serait présenté dans son établissement avant d’emmener la caissière ainsi que la recette du jour. Une initiative pour le moins surprenante, puisqu’il aurait ensuite retenu les deux pendant deux semaines à son domicile privé, sous couvert d’une prétendue garde à vue. Une tenue camouflée découverte au domicile Alertés par les plaintes, les policiers du commissariat de Kétou ont mené des investigations qui ont permis d’identifier et d’interpeller le suspect. La perquisition effectuée à son domicile a notamment permis de découvrir une tenue camouflée qu’il aurait utilisée pour se donner une apparence de policier. L’affaire met ainsi en lumière les risques liés à l’usurpation de la qualité d’agent des forces de l’ordre, mais aussi la facilité avec laquelle un uniforme peut servir à abuser de la confiance de citoyens peu méfiants. À l’issue de son interpellation, le suspect a été placé en garde à vue. Il est annoncé prochainement devant le procureur de la République pour répondre des faits qui lui sont reprochés. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Interpellation d'un faux policier qui plaçait ses victimes en «garde à vue» chez lui est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Trump asks Greece ambassador to resign amid ethics scandal
items.description: US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked its ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, to resign, the White House said on Tuesday, amid allegations that she sought money from a Trump supporter and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen. “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing. The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. “She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that “she will not be there”. In a statement on X, Guilfoyle rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece. “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she wrote. Guilfoyle thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president while acknowledging that her time as ambassador “may be coming to an end”. Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen. The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. “Honey, please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges. Luxury trips Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing. The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations. She travelled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper. Guilfoyle also spent Christmas at the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos, and stayed at a luxury Paris hotel on a trip with him, with Tsakos footing the bill, The Journal reported. The State Department’s inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports. The revelations emerged as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Europe last week, including a stop in Athens , where he declined to comment on the allegations. Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr ended. A former prosecutor and television commentator, she was previously married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom.

items.title: Akpabio insists on jail term for suicide attempt; bill scales second reading
items.description: By Henry Umoru Moves by the Senate to establish a framework for suicide prevention, decriminalise attempted suicide and provide for the establishment of persons who attempt suicide got a boost as the bill to this effect scaled second reading in the Senate. The bill scaled second despite the position of the President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio, who insisted that the act should remain punishable by imprisonment. Akpabio argued that removing the penalties could encourage the act, arguing thus, “If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail.” Akpabio added that the issue involves both the Criminal Code and the Penal Code, requiring input from State Houses of Assembly during a public hearing to avoid legal conflicts. The proposed bill seeks to remove the conflict between existing criminal laws that punish attempted suicide and the National Mental Health Act, which recognises the need for medical intervention in mental health emergencies, just as it seeks to address what he described as a contradiction in Nigeria’s laws. It is titled A Bill to establish framework for Suicide Prevention, decriminalise attempted suicide and provide for the establishment of persons who attempt suicide, and for related Matters 2006(SB.730) it was sponsored by Senator Ekpenyong Asuquo, APC, Cross River South. The bill was on Tuesday referred to the Senate Committee on Health ( Secondary and Tertiary) and Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters for further legislative action. In his lead debate on the general principles of the bill, Senator Asuquo explained that the proposed amendment would establish a legal framework for suicide prevention, treatment and support for people who survive suicide attempts, and that the central question before the Senate was whether the state should punish or protect a person who survives an attempt to take their own life. Ekpenyong argued that while the National Mental Health Act recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring treatment, Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code still criminalise the act. He said the proposed legislation would replace punitive responses with appropriate medical assessment, treatment and continuing support for survivors. “The police station or correctional facility should not be the default destination for a person who requires urgent clinical care,” Ekpenyong said. “At the heart of this bill is a simple question. When a Nigerian survives a suicide attempt, should the first response of the state be persecution or protection?” he asked. Ekpenyong, who noted that while the National Mental Health Act recognised attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate intervention, Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code continued to expose survivors to criminal punishment, said, “Our law presently speaks with two voices,” arguing that the contradiction needed to be resolved to ensure that people experiencing mental health crises received appropriate care. He however warned that criminalising attempted suicide could discourage people from seeking help, encourage families to conceal incidents and prevent health workers from reporting cases promptly, adding that treating suicide attempts as criminal offences could also deepen the stigma surrounding mental health conditions and undermine efforts to gather reliable data for national suicide prevention programmes. Ekpenyong, who further explained that the bill would provide for coordinated suicide prevention services, crisis response mechanisms, referral pathways and support for people who survive suicide attempts, said it would also promote public education and training for health workers, teachers, law enforcement personnel and emergency responders to enable them to recognise warning signs and connect people at risk with appropriate services. According to him, decriminalisation alone would not be sufficient without accessible medical and psychological care, calling for institutional arrangements and funding to support the implementation of suicide prevention policies, just as he urged his colleagues to support the bill, saying Nigeria needed a system that recognised distress and responded before a crisis became irreversible. Supporting the proposal, lawmakers argued that survivors of suicide attempts should receive medical and psychological care rather than face criminal prosecution. In his contribution, Senator Dayo Faduyile, APC, Ondo South, who cited his experience practising medicine, said attempted suicide should be approached as a medical emergency rather than a criminal offence, and argued that depression and other mental health conditions could impair a person’s judgement, making it necessary to prioritise treatment and recovery. The senator, who noted that some people who survived suicide attempts had subsequently taken their lives while in detention, warned that imprisonment or police custody could not adequately address the underlying medical condition, adding, “The best way to treat anybody who did not succumb to a suicide attempt is actually not to criminalise it. They need help.” According to him, placing people experiencing such crises in police stations or correctional facilities would not resolve their problems, insisting that they required proper medical attention. Also in his contribution, Senator Abdul Ningi, Bauchi Central, who hailed Ekpenyong for bringing the issue before the Senate, describing it as an important legal and public health debate that had not received sufficient attention, said the second reading would allow the proposal to proceed for further scrutiny, public consultation and contributions from professionals and other stakeholders. According to him, the circumstances surrounding suicide attempts required a broader understanding of mental health and the social pressures confronting individuals, adding that the proposed legislation would provide an opportunity for psychologists, medical practitioners and other experts to contribute to the development of a more effective national response. Ningi said people responded differently to life’s difficulties and that those who could not cope with particular circumstances should not automatically be treated as criminals. In his contribution, the Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, APC, Ekiti Central, however, cautioned that some provisions of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act were not automatically applicable across all states, depending on the legal framework adopted by their respective Houses of Assembly. According to him, the Senate needed to establish the extent to which the proposed amendment would apply nationally before proceeding with the legislation. The post Akpabio insists on jail term for suicide attempt; bill scales second reading appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Incredible Ambitions, and Rivalry, of Musk and Bezos
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Back in March 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency, led by Elon Musk, dropped news in the dead of night. “Good work by @NASA this week,” the post said. “Eliminated their unused purchasing Cards (~80%) -Terminated ~$420M in unneeded contracts, including $45M ($15m each) to three separate consultants.” The irony should not require explanation, but as my colleague Josh Tyrangiel details in his new cover story, Musk’s company, SpaceX, might not exist today without the $1.6 billion contract it received from NASA back in 2008, when it was days away from missing payroll, to resupply the International Space Station. “The company had gone from near death to indispensable in a single quarter,” Tyrangiel writes. Musk’s space ambitions are no secret—and they are matched, perhaps, only by the ambitions of Amazon’s founder, Jeff Bezos. In 2018, a decade after Musk’s company became the first private one to launch a liquid-fueled rocket into space, Bezos said the only way to “deploy this much financial resource is by converting my Amazon winnings into space travel. That is basically it.” Private individuals have long been a part of America’s relationship with space, but the nation is now reliant on one or two people to ensure that they can achieve the goals they set. On Radio Atlantic , Josh joins me to talk about how the relationship between NASA and these companies developed, the competition between the two men, and what it means for all of us down here on Earth. The following is a transcript of the episode: Josh Tyrangiel: Part of what Musk and Bezos are seeing is that right now space is an okay business. It’s not great. Satellites: better business. But down the road, if you can get satellites connected to data centers in space, and you have AI models that are super thirsty for computing power and for energy, all of a sudden you have a very virtuous loop that makes it really hard to compete with you in any part of that vertically integrated business. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to talk about the new space race. Public and private partnerships have defined the nation’s relationship with space for a long time. Some of the 20th century’s earliest astronomical discoveries would not have been possible without financial support from Andrew Carnegie. Now the future of space exploration finds itself at the behest of a trillionaire and a multi- billionaire, Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, and their companies SpaceX and Blue Origin. Over the last two decades, the two have become indispensable to NASA. If they can put aside their intense rivalry, it could benefit America’s new frontier into space. But what is the future of space exploration if they don’t? Today, I’m joined by my colleague Josh Tyrangiel, whose story in this month’s issue of The Atlantic explores both companies and the men who run them. Let’s get to questions. Josh, thank you so much for joining me today. Tyrangiel: Oh, it’s my pleasure. Thanks for having me, Adam. Harris: Absolutely. Can you first just sort of lay a foundation for us, right? We have Musk and SpaceX, Bezos and Blue Origin, and both are building capacity for literal moonshots and beyond, right? But what can they actually do right now? Tyrangiel: So where they are right now is that SpaceX is indispensable and critical infrastructure for the United States of America. It is how we get astronauts and materials to the International Space Station, which is really important. That’s how we get our—getting rides up there is really pretty, pretty great. The other thing that SpaceX does incredibly well is launch satellites. And so when Elon Musk was beginning SpaceX, he really pursued it actually just as a, almost as a kind of lark. He had made some money from PayPal. He was always fascinated with space, and he thought he wanted to do this kind of, like, science experiment/publicity stunt where he would get a rocket, send it to Mars, put a robot on it, scoop up some soil, and plant the first interstellar plant. And what he discovered was that actually, it’s really expensive to buy a rocket. He went to the Russians. One of the Russians literally spat on his shoes. And so he built this rocket capacity, and we can talk about how he did it, but what he discovered pretty quickly is, like, it’s not a great business, launching rockets. It’s very expensive. There aren’t—there isn’t that much demand. And so about 10 years ago he figured out that where there is a lot of demand is telecom, like, good old-fashioned telecom, and that became Starlink, which is a really incredible product. He has—most of the satellites in the world, he has launched through SpaceX. I believe the number is about, 80 percent of the mass in orbit is launched, has been launched by SpaceX, which is shocking. The next-closest competitor is the government of China. So when you say, like, What can they do now? Well, SpaceX kinda runs space, like, pretty clearly. Now, Blue Origin, for all sorts of reasons, got off to a much slower start, and right now it is trying to get in the game as a competitor, largely around launch, largely around the ability to launch satellites both for itself—Amazon has satellites; Blue Origin has launched a satellite project—but also for other customers. And there are a lot of space-satellite customers out there. And it’s also working on a lunar lander for NASA that might get there by 2030. But they’re far behind, and even the CEO of Blue Origin would be the first to tell you, like, it’s not a close competition at the moment. But these two are pretty important players in the space ecosystem. Without SpaceX, you would notice. You would actually notice both from a government point of view and from a satellite point of view. Harris: I thought it was interesting—earlier, you mentioned space travel is expensive at, like, a very base minimum, right? And really any piece about space exploration, I feel like I always get kind of bogged down in the numbers, because they just don’t compute. They seem fake, right? $50 billion here, $4 billion there. This is a lot of money to spend on something that’s not necessarily ever a guarantee. There’s no guarantee you make it to the moon. There’s no guarantee you make it to Mars. Why is space travel and the sort of space exploration, these space pursuits still worthy pursuits? Why are they still worthy pursuits? Tyrangiel: It’s a great question, and if you talk to people in the scientific or the, sort of, NASA community, there’s a healthy debate about, what’s the right return on investment? Let’s say it was your money, right? And you wanted to understand more about space. You could create vehicles. You could have an astronaut program. You could take on the tremendous risk to loss of life, which you don’t want. Or you could send drones. And one of the great programs right now that very few people know about is we have these two vehicles on Mars sending back photos every day that are just astonishing. It’s not an expensive program. We’re learning things about that planet that frankly—you know, if we were to wait for a human to get there, we’d be decades away. Not to mention, like, wouldn’t get them nearly as far. So there is a debate about that. What I would say is that if you are a captain of industry and you can afford to take some pain, there’s nothing better than losing money early to create a moat around a business that at some point might be transformed from bad to incredible. And so part of what Musk and Bezos are seeing is that right now space is an okay business. It’s not great. Satellites: better business. But down the road, if you can get satellites connected to data centers in space, and you have AI models that are super thirsty for computing power and for energy, all of a sudden you have a very virtuous loop that makes it really hard to compete with you in any part of that vertically integrated business. And so, I go back to the SpaceX prospectus, which I think I referred to in the piece as, like, kind of this incredible document that, in parts, seems like a very rational plan for how to colonize space, for how to make the East India Company of space, and, in other parts, seems like a diary of a CFO’s weekend on mushrooms, right? Like, it’s crazy. But when they say that SpaceX has a total addressable market of about $30 trillion, what they mean ultimately is creating this kind of vertically integrated loop where rockets launch satellites and data centers; data centers go through the satellites to feed compute back to Earth, running these AI models that run all of our heavy industry; and all of a sudden what looks like a lousy investment becomes an incredible investment. And so that is how both of those men think. That’s why to people like you and me it’s like, Boy, that’s a lot of money going out the door right now . They are not worried about “right now.” Harris: You know, and they often, sometimes they will, in order to talk about the investment, right, they will couch it in the civilizational concerns, right? Our resources are finite here on Earth. We’re going to need to find another place . In the colonizer mind, it’s like, We are going to colonize the moon next as a sort of base to begin to look elsewhere . Do they both have that sort of civilizational concern? Is that a real concern of theirs or is it just a— Tyrangiel: No, 100 percent sincere. I genuinely think that both men look at the state of the planet and very scientifically think, Okay, well, we need an off-ramp. In Bezos’s mind, it’s really O’Neill colonies, which is—Gerard O’Neill, in the 1970s, created this notion that you basically export all of our most polluting industries into space or onto the moon and then you kinda turn the planet into this beautiful park. And Bezos has been talking about this as long ago as his high-school-graduation speech. So he’s very sincerely focused on this notion. Musk largely thinks about Mars in the same way, which is that we need to become an interplanetary species. That doesn’t mean they also don’t see a tremendous business opportunity. And it doesn’t mean that the rest of us, who haven’t really, um, had much say in how these resources are being allocated or whether we would prefer, in fact, that we actually just work on saving this planet—it doesn’t mean that we can’t be annoyed about it, frustrated about it. But I think all of those things are true in this case. Harris: Could the government achieve any of the SpaceX ambitions, um, on its own? Or does it need these, sort of, mega-wealthy people in order to achieve what it’s trying to do? Tyrangiel: You know, it’s funny. When I, um, started reporting the story and I really dove deep into the subculture of space and government and heavy industry—you know, to a person, almost everyone agrees that the Commercial Space Act, or COTS, is one of the best pieces of public policy the United States has created in the last 40 years. And that basically what it did was create competition where previously there was bureaucracy, right? And so as a result, I think without question people would say Musk has made space move faster and farther, often at a discount to the federal government, and so that’s great, right? We actually wanna encourage that. And by the way, as much as these are complicated and at times troubling guys, we also want people who dream this big, and we want them to be in America, right? It’s great; it’s great. We want that. The challenge of course is, where do you draw the line about authority? And so what, what I saw and what we’ve seen in the last five, 10 years, is that when you control things like Starlink, you also control things like war. That puts us in a very, very strange place. Harris: You made this argument at the beginning, right, which is just the sort of reality of SpaceX being so far ahead of Blue Origin. What’s the best argument for hoping that Blue Origin catches up to SpaceX, and what would it look like for Blue Origin to catch up to SpaceX here? Tyrangiel : So I’ll tell you what the CEO, who’s a guy named Dave Limp, told me. And Dave Limp worked for Bezos at Amazon for somewhere between a decade and decade and a half. Knows him extremely well, which is a very important part of making Blue Origin successful, right? Is channeling what Bezos wants, being able to challenge him when necessary. So Dave Limp said, Look, SpaceX is ahead. But we don’t need them to fail for us to be successful. What we need is for there to be reasonable competition in the market for space launch, right? And right now Blue Origin needs to get its act together. And what I mean by that is they’ve been at it for about 26 years. And they’re just getting to a place where they are launching, landing reusable rockets, which is the key to driving down the cost. When you’re launching a new rocket or experimenting with a new booster or a new engine, one in three is gonna fail, right? And it takes time. I think the thing that we most want to root for is for Blue Origin to get on a cadence where it is driving down cost, getting competition, right? Getting other competitors, satellites, and other things into space beyond their own, right? What we don’t want is an environment where SpaceX controls most of the launch in the United States and most of its payloads are Starlink satellites or future AI satellites, and we don’t want that on the Blue Origin side. Now, we have lots of ways to make sure that people don’t have that kind of monopoly. But we’re not exactly in a moment where the Department of Justice is exercising those. You know, it’d be healthy for America to have, uh, two big competitors. It’d be healthier to have four, healthier still to have eight. Harris: When we come back, we talk to Josh about America’s ambitions in space, and whether or not they overlap with Musk and Bezos’s own ambitions. [ Music ] Harris: For the last half century, NASA has been the, sort of, benchmark for American ambition in space, and I’m often reminded of John F. Kennedy’s speech in 1962, his moonshot speech, where he says— John F. Kennedy: But why , some say, the moon? Why choose this as our goal? And they may well ask, Why climb the highest mountain? Why, 35 years ago, fly the Atlantic? Why does Rice play Texas? We choose to go to the moon. We choose to go to the moon. Harris: We choose to go to the moon because it was the hard thing to do. Not because it’s easy, but because it’s hard. What is America’s ambition now in space? Tyrangiel: So there’s a new NASA administrator named Jared Isaacman, and Isaacman had a tough time getting confirmed, in part because he’s a self-made billionaire, and he was a SpaceX pilot. He did the first commercial space walk in history, and so his ties to Musk were an issue in his confirmation hearing. But he did get confirmed. And everybody I speak to about Isaacman says, He’s young; he’s eager; he is all in on the mission . And they don’t always love his decisions, but they think he is a legit leader. And what he’s trying to organize everybody around is the moon. He wants American boots on the moon by 2028, and so he’s pressing Blue Origin, which is making a lander; he’s pressing SpaceX, which is making a lander. He wants both in competition, and ultimately, the reasons for that are sort of a, this kind of hairball, right? Some of it’s national security, the dark side of the moon. There are people in the national-security community who say, Well, we need to get there before China does. There are others who say, Not really, and, and that when they talk to China, it’s not actually that big a deal. But there are good reasons to go back. There’s mining on the moon. There’s rare earth minerals on the moon. And there is beginning to be this kind of space economy developing around the possibility of us getting to the moon, mining it, setting up data centers. There’s lots of buzz about nuclear reactors on the moon. That seems a little scary to me, but nevertheless that buzz is there. And so Isaacman has them pointed in that direction. And, and one interesting thing—we’re at this kind of lucky moment for America. Basically, you know, Blue Origin said, Well, let’s go to the moon . Trump sees the MAGA value in the moon. It appealed to Mike Pence, who really loves spaces. But— Harris: The creation of the Space Force. Tyrangiel: Yeah. Most of the time what happens is a NASA mission gets created, and four or eight years later, it gets dumped. And the Biden administration had the, kind of, unsung civil-service hero who was on the transition team, named Bhavya Lal, who’s a really a fascinating woman, and the administration came in, and Biden’s team said, Well, this, this is probably stupid, right? She’s like, No, no, no, no. It’s not stupid.Stay the course. And so we’ve had, for the last 10 years, actual continuity, and that is incredibly rare. And so what Isaacman has been very shrewd about is staying as close to the political middle as he can because he knows space deadlines are kinda worse than New Year’s resolutions. Like, I don’t know of anybody who looks at a space deadline as, like, Cool, let me make sure I’m there on that date. It just doesn’t happen. So knowing that it’s likely to slip, he’s been very shrewd about positioning himself in the middle so that if there is a new party in power, the moon mission might actually persevere, and that’s a hugely important thing to us getting back to the moon. Harris: Yeah. That sort of consistent goal. And we have that—I know that they’ve had that pretty consistent goal of getting back to the moon by 2028 with the Artemis crew. What role will Musk and Bezos, sort of, play in that mission specifically? Tyrangiel: I mean, one of them would like to win to carry those astronauts on a Blue Origin or a SpaceX lander to the moon—to the surface of the moon, which you can imagine, if you’ve been working at this for a quarter century, would be a huge personal and professional triumph. So they’re very invested in that. Whether that competition is the right thing for the United States I think is a little bit debatable. How Isaacman approaches declaring a winner—he did not speak to me for the piece, but, like, it is a subject of heated debate inside the space community. It’s like, Which one of these vehicles is actually right for this? Are either of them right for this? And how do we choose a winner here when both have tremendous political influence? Harris: Thinking about that idea of a winner too—you write in the piece about the ways that if they just worked together, right, we, we all might be in a better place. Is there a world in which Musk and Bezos do actually work together? Tyrangiel: The answer is no, definitively. They’re not gonna work together voluntarily. It’s just not gonna happen. And by the way, we do want them in competition because that competition drives price down, that competition drives creativity. Like, I think that’s great. What we also want is a federal government that can remind what are essentially—forget the billions attached to them, forget their outsize personalities and profiles. They’re vendors, right? We want our federal government to be able to say Okay , and, and this is really where I get to, not to spoil the piece because obviously I know people have been reading it while we’re talking, but basically when you look at, um, SpaceX’s plan for how to get to the moon, and you look at Blue Origin’s plan, they’re quite complementary. SpaceX does one thing extraordinarily well. Blue does one thing extraordinarily well. Jared Isaacman could very easily say, Okay, SpaceX, you’re gonna be the refueler. Blue, you’re gonna be the lander. Work together or do nothing. Right? That’s what we’d love to see. It’s just an exercise in reminding everybody the nation matters more than people’s egos or people’s business plans. The problem with that is that while the leverage we have is the glory of getting to the moon, the leverage each individual has is to say, Screw you! I don’t wanna go to the moon. And guess what? Then we’re not getting to the moon. And so that’s back to the sort of original piece of this, which is, we’re in this weird moment where we have empowered the space race; we have given federal money to these companies; we’ve given them lots and lots of support, even down to the educational system, which produces so many of the engineers working at these companies. But we’re not entirely in control of their ambitions. And even with something like the moon—you know, if they decide it’s not economically feasible, if they decide they don’t wanna work together, all that leverage is gone and we’re not getting back to the moon. Harris: Even if the government threatens to revoke their contracts, they could just say, We have more money than that. We don’t need your contract ? Tyrangiel : So, at some point, yes, right? And SpaceX is not—SpaceX gets money from the government, but SpaceX is also funneling lots of its own money in, and it also is the launch provider of choice to satellite companies. So yeah, there is a moment at which we lose control of these companies. Now, traditionally, we have things like the Defense Production Act. You can nationalize things. I don’t think there’s any political will for that at this moment, and so we’re navigating this really awkward conversation across the table with two guys who are not used to negotiating, giving in, working together, and so it will have an impact on our national ambitions at some point. Like, I think that’s inevitable. Harris: Yeah. And there’s no way out of it? We’re stuck with our two billionaires/occasional trillionaire? Tyrangiel: I mean, we can continue to encourage competitors, and there are a lot of space start-ups, but they’re pretty far away from being mature enough to compete with SpaceX, let alone Blue Origin. So for the time being, meaning the rest of my adult life, I imagine this is how we’ll be dealing with space. Yeah. Harris: Well, Josh, thank you so much for taking the time to chat with me. You’ve given us a lot to think about, and as always, it’s great to talk to you. Tyrangiel: Great to talk to you. Thanks for having me. [ Music ] Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.
